clue.text: Commitment that may be shown by author at the start

definitions.meaning: first meaning: devotion to a task or cause

definitions.text: that may be shown by author at the start
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the line a writer puts on an opening page offering the book to someone

explanation.surface: A writer shows how committed they are right from the opening of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads like more about commitment, but it is a separate meaning: the 'To my wife' line printed before the first chapter.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both steadfast devotion to something and the inscription a writer places in front of a book honouring a person.

clue.text: I ordered up hams, cheeses etc

definitions.note: the clue lists the goods sold rather than the shop, a loose but common way of defining a delicatessen

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, the opposite of the usual direction

parts.note: taken as written
to lead troops is to order them about, so ordered = led

explanation.surface: Someone says they have put in an order for cold meats and cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered up' looks like a phrase about buying, but 'up' turns the letters round, which works because this is a down entry read from the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A delicatessen is the shop known for cured meats, cheeses and similar prepared foods, so the goods stand in for the counter.

clue.text: Lay out 52 cards

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to knock someone flat with a punch
second meaning: a full pack of playing cards

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests dealing out a pack for patience; 'Lay out' is really slang for floor someone with a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: As a slang verb it means punch someone to the ground, and as a noun it is the complete pack of fifty-two playing cards.

clue.text: Darts star cut out pastries

indicators.note: letters that are out of place are no longer in their proper order

parts.note: all twelve letters of the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A darts champion snubs the pastries, cutting them from the diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut out' reads as a phrase meaning dropped, but 'cut' is part of the material and only 'out' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: These are small baked shells filled with set egg cream, a classic bakery item and so a kind of pastry.

clue.text: Easy to spook with tail of newt, cackling and casting spells?

indicators.note: an animal's tail is at its back end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the word
cackling and spell-casting are what a witch does, so behaving like one

explanation.surface: A witch's brew of newt and spells makes something nervous and jumpy.
explanation.walkthrough: Eye of newt belongs in a witch's cauldron, so the surface hangs together; the question mark flags that WITCHY is an invented description rather than a dictionary synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone nervous and jumpy is easily startled, so being readily frightened is exactly that jittery state.

clue.text: Catastrophe. Liaison. She's part of both?

indicators.note: being part of two words means spanning the end of one and the start of the next

parts.note: the letters run on across the full stop, from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Two one-word headlines, and a woman who figures in both.
explanation.walkthrough: The full stops seem to split the clue into separate items, but the hidden name runs straight across them. Hamlet's Ophelia is part of his tragic catastrophe and of a doomed liaison with him.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun points at a female character, and this heroine of Hamlet is a woman, so a single named she fills the gap.

clue.text: Newts somewhat bereft, sadly

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only a portion of the following letters is wanted

parts.note: the letters run consecutively from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Some newts have been left bereaved and sad.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a sense of bereavement, but 'bereft, sadly' is only where the letters sit. An eft is an old and crossword-favoured word for a newt.
explanation.definitionFit: An eft is a newt, especially a young land-dwelling one, a word now met mostly in crosswords.

clue.text: Haunt deserted library many a time

parts.note: to haunt a place is to visit it often

indicators.note: a deserted building has nobody inside, so the interior letters are emptied out and only the ends stay

parts.note: just the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A ghost repeatedly haunts an abandoned library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haunt' suggests a ghost, but it is the ordinary verb for visiting a place habitually.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens on many occasions happens often, which is the adverb's plain meaning.

clue.text: We see rent's adjusted, suggesting bribery

definitions.note: the answer is a plural noun for bribes while 'bribery' is the practice, a mass noun standing for the payments it involves

indicators.note: adjusting something changes its arrangement, so the letters are moved about

parts.note: the letters of all three words, the S of the possessive included

explanation.surface: Tenants notice their rent has been changed and suspect someone was paid off.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S looks like grammar, but its S is part of the material.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetener is slang for an inducement or bribe, a payment slipped across to win favour.

clue.text: Tradespersons related fables about hair?

indicators.note: tales about a subject name that subject first, so the topic comes before the tales
to relate a story is to tell it out loud, so what follows is heard rather than read

parts.note: locks are tresses of hair
fables are myths; the S of the first word slides across in speech

explanation.surface: Craftsmen telling folk tales about hairstyles.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'locks myths' and you hear LOCKSMITHS: the S simply moves from one word to the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Locksmiths are skilled workers who make and repair locks and keys, so they are a kind of tradesperson.

clue.text: Blessed ecclesiast, divine educator primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so each word gives up its opening letter

parts.note: one letter from the front of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A description of a holy churchman who was above all a teacher of theology.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the source of the letters. The Venerable Bede was an Anglo-Saxon monk and scholar, a churchman and teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: This eighth-century Northumbrian monk wrote history and theology and is venerated as a saint and Doctor of the Church.

clue.text: Means of making people believe lingerie not ready to wear?

parts.note: a piece of underwear
a garment still at the laundry stage cannot be put on yet

explanation.surface: A con trick to convince people that underwear isn't fit to put on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lingerie not ready to wear' reads as fashion talk, but it is a bra in the washing; the question mark marks that playful phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Indoctrination by pressure and repetition is a method used to force beliefs onto people, which is what the phrase describes.

clue.text: Author's representation of corrupt males

indicators.note: a representation shows something in a new form, so the letters are recast

parts.note: all twelve letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A novelist's portrayal of morally rotten men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' looks like the shuffle signal sitting next to its material, but it is part of the material; 'representation of' does the reshaping.
explanation.definitionFit: This French novelist wrote In Search of Lost Time, so he is a famous writer.

clue.text: Characteristics? They're sometimes detached

definitions.meaning: first meaning: qualities or attributes of something
second meaning: buildings for sale, some of which stand apart from their neighbours

explanation.walkthrough: 'Detached' suggests aloof people, but estate agents describe houses with no shared walls as detached.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means traits or attributes, and it is also the estate-agent word for houses and buildings, which may stand alone.

clue.text: Having stopped work to eat bananas

definitions.meaning: first meaning: away from the desk for a midday meal

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has someone taking a break to eat fruit; 'bananas' is really the slang adjective for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally describes someone away for a midday meal, and idiomatically means crazy or not all there.

clue.text: Run, with good reason, heading off forcefully

indicators.note: with its heading gone, a word loses its first letter

parts.note: R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run
to argue soundly is to argue with good reason; its front letter then goes

explanation.surface: Someone hurries off, with good cause, in a determined manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With good reason' is an adverb phrase meaning SOUNDLY; drop its first letter and attach it after the run.
explanation.definitionFit: To be criticised roundly is to be criticised bluntly and vigorously, so the adverb means in a vigorous, emphatic way.

clue.text: Somewhere on the Rhône, American wanting six starters of grits and nachos receiving disagreeable response

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for American
six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: starters come first in a meal, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of the two foods
a refusal is a response that does not agree

explanation.surface: An American in a French town asks for grits and nachos and is told no.
explanation.walkthrough: The refusal sits between the two food initials. Avignon is a city on the Rhône in southern France, once home to the popes.
explanation.definitionFit: The city of the papal palace and the famous bridge stands on the Rhône river in Provence, so it is a place on that river.

clue.text: Honey, perhaps, that one may give to boxer

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an affectionate word for a loved one

definitions.text: that one may give to boxer
definitions.meaning: second meaning: what an owner calls a dog of the boxer breed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxer' looks like a fighter and 'give' like a punch, but a boxer is also a breed of dog, which needs a name.
explanation.definitionFit: A term of endearment like darling is one sense, and a name chosen for a household animal is the literal other.

clue.text: In the auditorium, Everyman becomes tedious, displaying spectacles etc

indicators.note: an auditorium is a place for listening, so the sound of a word is wanted

parts.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I
something that palls begins to wear on you, or wear thin

explanation.surface: At the theatre, the setter grows boring while showing off glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's name in a clue usually means I or ME; heard aloud, I is EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasses, goggles and contact lenses all count as gear worn for the eyes, a collective noun for such items.

clue.text: Crow, lazy sort, leaving island: one's slow to move

parts.note: a daw, or jackdaw, is a member of the crow family

indicators.note: something that leaves is no longer there, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: an idle person
I is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A lazy bird finally leaves the island, taking its time about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The island's I comes off the front of the lazy sort before it joins the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dawdles lingers and lags behind, so such a person is sluggish to get going.

clue.text: Doctor's operation on pedestrian that's fallen

parts.note: DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor
OP is short for operation
PED is an abbreviation for pedestrian, as in ped crossing

explanation.surface: A doctor operates on a pedestrian who has had a fall.
explanation.walkthrough: Every piece is a standard short form, laid out in the order the clue gives them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something that has come down, as with prices or a stitch let go, so the past participles match.

clue.text: Bizarrely, our tree sloth is to be in control

indicators.note: something bizarre is strange and out of the ordinary, so the letters are put in an odd order

parts.note: all twelve letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Strangely, the sloth in our tree is going to be the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: A sloth hangs in a tree and is the least commanding animal imaginable, which is the joke of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from the cockerel dominating the henhouse, and means to be the dominant person in charge.

clue.text: Flooring — as nothing, twice, is recalled

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters come back the other way

parts.note: the figure zero looks like the letter O
nothing a second time, this time as the score word for zero

explanation.surface: A floor covering being called back, as if it counted for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing, twice' asks for two different words for zero, set side by side and then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Lino is the short form of linoleum, a hard-wearing sheet floor covering.

clue.text: This person is seen around opening of mosque?

definitions.text: This person is seen around opening of mosque?

indicators.note: being around something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: a speaker describing themselves would say 'I am'

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its front, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A figure regularly spotted near the doorway of a mosque.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: an imam leads prayers and is naturally found at a mosque.
explanation.definitionFit: An imam is the man who leads prayers in a mosque, so he is the person you would expect to see there.

clue.text: Where to drink in Nova Scotia

parts.note: taken as written
NS is the postal abbreviation for the Canadian province

explanation.surface: Asking for the bars in a Canadian province.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word placing the drinking in Canada, but it supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Inns are pubs and taverns, establishments serving alcohol, so they are places one goes for a drink.

clue.text: Flower arrangement of lupin with heads of marguerite daisy, English iris and hollyhock

indicators.note: to arrange items is to set them out in a chosen order, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a head is at the top, so each word gives its first letter

parts.words: marguerite daisy, English iris and hollyhock
parts.note: the initials of the five words, 'and' aside

explanation.surface: A florist's arrangement combining lupins with daisies, irises and hollyhocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower arrangement' reads as one phrase, but it splits: the first word is the definition and 'arrangement of' signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: The delphinium, or larkspur, is a tall garden plant with spikes of blue blooms.

clue.text: Shop regularly; shop in the centre where Carnaby St.'s found

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept

parts.note: the first and third letters

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so only the inner letters are kept

parts.note: the two letters between the ends

explanation.surface: Advice to go shopping often in the heart of London's fashion district.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word is used twice with different selections. Carnaby Street is a famous shopping street in Soho, in London's West End.
explanation.definitionFit: This central London district contains Carnaby Street, the shopping street famous since the 1960s, so it is the area where that street lies.

clue.text: Bachelor with fair feature to smarten up — because he's this

definitions.text: Bachelor with fair feature to smarten up — because he's this

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in BA
a fairground attraction such as a carousel
to groom yourself is to tidy your appearance

explanation.surface: A single man with good looks tidies himself up for a reason that the clue leaves us to name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair feature' suggests a handsome face, but the fair is a funfair. Read whole, the clue describes a bachelor sprucing up for his wedding day.
explanation.definitionFit: A man about to be married is still a bachelor who dresses up smartly for the ceremony, which is what the full sentence describes.
